notes.why: A shadow as an event (a flinch when the frame darkens), and the moon's phase from the date (Lin 2021; Levy 2007). Not drawn; graded i if added.
Starfish look out from each arm at once (a flat band 100 by 30 degrees each); scallops and giant clams have rows of small eyes. Not drawn.

rows: Sea anemones and corals have no eyes. The picture keeps only how much light there is, what colour it is and where it comes from.

A reef coral makes more of one blue-light pigment on full-moon nights than on new-moon nights. Hundreds of kinds of coral spawn together on a few nights each year, and moonlight helps set those nights.
One reef coral spawns after the moon starts rising late, leaving a stretch of darkness after sunset. A dim light of about 0.3 lux at night held its spawning back.
A small sea anemone released its eggs and sperm in step only when blue light, standing in for a full moon, shone through five nights of each month. White light did little.
A surf clam has a nerve that senses light by itself. When a shadow falls, the nerve fires a burst and the clam pulls in its siphon.
A moon jelly has small cups of light-sensing cells around its rim, and it swims faster in brighter light. Without those cups it no longer does.
A scallop has up to 200 eyes along the edge of its shell, each focusing light with a mirror, and a giant clam has several hundred pinhole eyes. This view does not draw them.
Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, some with lenses, and one kind looks up through the water to steer by the trees above it. This view does not draw them.
A starfish has an eye at the tip of each arm. In the crown-of-thorns starfish each eye has about 250 tiny facets and looks out sideways over a patch about 100 degrees wide and 30 high.
The blue sea star is colour blind, and its eyes follow flicker only up to 1 or 2 times a second, against about 60 for yours. The starfish picture is grey, and anything that moves smears.
Garm and Nilsson 2014 (the 1 to 2 hertz is secondary)
A purple sea urchin has no eyes, yet it turned toward or away from a dark disc 10 degrees wide and ignored one 6.5 degrees wide. Its spines shade the light-sensitive cells between them.
The grey weights, the choice of a light-only picture for animals that have no eyes, and the slow pace of the starfish picture are the app's own.
With the moon option, the view at night is as bright as tonight's moon, worked out from the date. Many corals time their spawning by the moon; how the brightness follows it is the app's.
